categories.name: Encounter source: schedule or census
categories.summary: The list of who was seen, where and by whom. Office practices have an appointment schedule. Hospital, nursing facility and home-visit practices have a census or rounding list. Every billable encounter starts here, so gaps here never appear in any billing report.
good_looks_like: One list each day shows every patient seen, the site and the clinician.
Each day's list is compared with charges entered, and every difference is explained.
New admissions, discharges, transfers and deaths reach the list the same day.
For office practices, no-shows and cancellations are recorded and followed up.
failure_modes: A clinician sees patients who were never added to the census, and those visits are never billed.
A patient is discharged or dies and recurring charges continue.
Two lists exist, the facility's and the practice's, and nobody reconciles them.
Empty appointment slots and no-shows go unmeasured.
key_questions: Where does our list of patients seen come from, and who keeps it current?
How many encounters last month had no charge, and why?
How quickly do we learn of an admission, discharge or death?
What is our no-show rate, if we schedule visits?

actions.action: Reconcile the list to charges every day
actions.detail: Count encounters by site and clinician on the census or schedule, and compare with charges entered. List the gaps.

actions.action: Get facility census changes daily
actions.detail: Ask each facility for a daily admission, discharge and transfer report, or pull it from its portal.

actions.action: Close each day's list
actions.detail: The clinician confirms the list is complete before leaving the site or at day end.

actions.action: Track no-shows and fill gaps
actions.detail: For scheduled practices: reminders, a waiting list and a same-day standby list.

categories.applies_when: Every practice. Office practices work from a schedule and watch unfilled slots and no-shows. Facility-based and home-visit practices work from a census, where the risk is a visit made but never listed. Hospital-based specialists work from the hospital's census, operating room schedule or order log.

vendor_refs.note: One checklist question scores daily or weekly matching of completed encounters to posted charges. No method is given, and nothing covers a facility census or no-shows.
Recommends a monthly count of encounters against charges. Its statement that 1% to 3% of encounters typically go unbilled has no source.

categories.evidence_note: Reconciling the day's list to charges is an internal control by convention, not a regulation. The Healthcare Financial Management Association (HFMA) measures schedule use and charge delay, not reconciliation. No-show figures are Medical Group Management Association (MGMA) medians for 2025. Census accuracy has no benchmark.

metrics.name: Encounters reconciled to a charge or a documented reason
metrics.definition: Share of encounters on the schedule or census that have either a charge entered or a recorded reason for no charge.
metrics.formula: Encounters with a charge or documented reason / encounters on the schedule or census
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. The target from first principles is 100% within a few days of service.
metrics.data_hint: The scheduling or census tool compared with charges in the billing system.

metrics.name: No-show rate
metrics.definition: Share of scheduled appointments where the patient did not arrive and did not cancel in advance.
metrics.benchmark_typical: 5% to 7% by specialty group, 6% in primary care
metrics.benchmark_note: MGMA medians, 2025 data: primary care 6.0%, surgical 5.0%, nonsurgical specialties 7.0%. One in three groups reported higher no-shows in 2026 (MGMA poll). Applies to scheduled office practices, not to rounding practices.
metrics.data_hint: The scheduling system's appointment status report.

categories.name: Registration and demographic accuracy
categories.summary: Getting the patient's identity, insurance details and responsible party right at the start. A wrong birth date, subscriber number or name spelling is enough to reject a claim.
good_looks_like: Name, birth date, sex, address, subscriber number and plan are taken from the insurance card or an electronic eligibility answer, not typed from memory.
Required fields cannot be skipped.
For facility patients, the admission summary (face sheet) is obtained at admission and checked against eligibility.
A signed authorization to bill the insurer and be paid directly is on file. If a Medicare patient cannot sign, a guardian, relative or facility representative may (42 CFR 424.36).
failure_modes: Names and numbers are retyped from a faxed face sheet and one digit is wrong.
The patient's plan changed in January and the old card is still on file.
The responsible party for a patient with dementia is unknown, so statements go nowhere.
Registration errors are fixed claim by claim and never traced to their source.
key_questions: What share of our rejections and denials come from registration errors?
Do we verify identity and coverage electronically before the first claim?
For facility patients, who sends us the face sheet and how fast?
Do we know the responsible party for every patient who cannot manage their own affairs?

actions.action: Use the eligibility answer to correct registration
actions.detail: When the payer's electronic answer shows a different name, birth date or subscriber number, update the record to match.

actions.action: Make key fields required
actions.detail: Subscriber number, plan, birth date and responsible party before a claim can be created.

actions.action: Trace registration denials to their source
actions.detail: Each month, list rejections and denials caused by demographic errors and where each record came from.

actions.action: Get face sheets at admission
actions.detail: Agree with each facility on how and when the practice receives them.

categories.applies_when: Every practice. Practices with no front desk depend on facility face sheets, hospital registration data and electronic eligibility, so the accuracy check has to be built into intake of the census.

vendor_refs.note: Lists registration data to capture and how often to re-check it. Its 2% and 5% thresholds are unsourced, and it matches names to photo ID, not the payer's record.
Adds a weekly registration audit sheet and a pre-service queue. The sheets are empty tables: the status column has no formula, and nothing covers face sheets or facility patients.

categories.evidence_note: Convention, apart from the Medicare signature rule (42 CFR 424.36). No measured benchmark for registration accuracy in physician practices was found. The Healthcare Financial Management Association (HFMA) defines a pre-registration rate but sets no target. Survey context comes from Experian Health, a vendor (2026).

metrics.name: Claims rejected or denied for registration errors
metrics.definition: Share of claims rejected by the clearinghouse, the service that forwards claims to payers, or denied by the payer, because of patient identity, subscriber or demographic errors.
metrics.formula: Claims rejected or denied for registration reasons / claims submitted
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. For context, 43% of 204 surveyed provider staff said inaccurate registration data caused at least 5% of their denials (Experian Health, a vendor, 2026).
metrics.data_hint: Clearinghouse rejection reports, plus reason codes on the payer's payment report: 31 (patient not identified as insured) and 140 (identification number and name do not match).
metrics.vendor_claim: The purchased front-end playbook sets a target of under 2% of claims denied for registration reasons and calls over 5% a systematic problem.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Unverifiable. No source is given, and it counts payer denials only, missing the clearinghouse rejections where many of these errors surface.

categories.name: Eligibility and coverage discovery
categories.summary: Confirming, electronically, that the patient is covered on the date of service, by which plan, and what the patient will owe. For patients seen repeatedly, coverage must be checked again each month, because plans change.
good_looks_like: Eligibility is checked electronically before or on the date of service for every patient.
Patients under ongoing care are re-checked at the start of every month.
The full answer from the payer is stored as proof.
When no coverage is found, a search for other coverage, including Medicaid, is run before the patient is treated as self-pay.
Staff also confirm the plan type, that the clinician is in the plan's network, and whether a referral or authorization is needed.
failure_modes: Coverage is checked once at intake and never again, so a January plan change produces months of denials.
Staff check coverage by phone or portal for payers that answer electronically.
A charge is entered with no payer and sits unbilled.
A patient is billed as self-pay when Medicaid or a Medicare plan was active.
key_questions: What share of encounters have an electronic eligibility check on file?
Do we re-check every active patient each month?
How many charges last month had no payer when entered?
What share of our denials are for coverage that had ended or another payer being responsible?

actions.action: Check eligibility electronically for every encounter
actions.detail: Use the billing system or a clearinghouse connection. Reserve phone and portal checks for payers with no electronic answer.

actions.action: Re-verify all active patients monthly
actions.detail: Run the whole active list on the first business day. Medicare's answer shows Medicare Advantage enrollment, another primary payer, hospice periods and Qualified Medicare Beneficiary status. Flag every change.

actions.action: Hold claims with no verified payer
actions.detail: A short daily list of encounters with no confirmed coverage, worked until empty.

actions.action: Search for coverage before billing self-pay
actions.detail: Medicare's contractor portal can find a patient's Medicare number from name, birth date and Social Security number. Also check the state Medicaid portal and any coverage search your clearinghouse offers.

categories.applies_when: Every practice. Monthly re-verification matters most where patients are seen repeatedly and can change plans in any month, as nursing facility residents and people with both Medicare and Medicaid can (42 CFR 422.62 and 423.38). Hospital-based practices get coverage from the hospital's registration and should re-check it before billing.

vendor_refs.note: Lists what to read in the payer's answer and re-checks coverage at every visit. Its figure of 20% to 30% of self-pay patients with hidden coverage has no source.
Adds a re-verification log recording stage, date, source and result of each check. It has no fields for Medicare Advantage enrollment, hospice or patients who may not be billed.

categories.evidence_note: Health plans must answer an electronic eligibility inquiry (45 CFR 162.925). CAQH's yearly industry survey measured the cost of each method. The Healthcare Financial Management Association (HFMA) defines the verification rate and sets no target. The common 98% target traces to a vendor white paper.

metrics.name: Encounters with eligibility verified
metrics.definition: Share of encounters for which coverage was confirmed with the payer for the date of service, before the claim was sent.
metrics.formula: Encounters with a stored eligibility confirmation / encounters
metrics.benchmark_note: HFMA defines the measure and publishes no target. Aim for every encounter. Provider cost per check (CAQH, 2023 data): $2.00 and 4 minutes electronic, $4.46 and 8 minutes by portal, $8.57 and 16 minutes by phone or fax.
metrics.data_hint: Eligibility transaction logs matched to encounters.
metrics.vendor_claim: The purchased front-end playbook says the rate should approach 100% and treats under 95% as a workflow failure. Other documents in the library use 80% or 85% as the alarm line.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Unverifiable. No document cites a source and the thresholds disagree with each other. The direction is right.

metrics.name: Denials for coverage or eligibility
metrics.definition: Share of claims denied because coverage had ended, had not begun, or the patient was not eligible for the service on that date.
metrics.formula: Claims denied for eligibility reasons / claims processed by payers
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend by payer. Many of these denials can be prevented by a check on the date of service, so a rising share deserves a root-cause look. Retroactive plan changes cannot be prevented.
metrics.data_hint: Denial reason codes on the payer's payment report: 26 (before coverage began), 27 (after coverage ended), 200 (lapse in coverage) and 177 (eligibility requirements not met).

metrics.name: Encounters with no payer on file at charge entry
metrics.definition: Share of encounters that reach charge entry, the step where the visit's billing codes are recorded, with no identified, verified payer.
metrics.formula: Encounters with no payer at charge entry / encounters
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. The target from first principles is close to zero, with a daily list of exceptions.
metrics.data_hint: A billing system report of charges with blank or unverified insurance.

categories.name: Coverage status that changes who pays
categories.summary: Facts about a patient on the date of service that change the payer, the place of service or whether a service is payable: a Medicare Part A skilled stay, hospice election, Medicare Advantage enrollment, another primary payer, and Qualified Medicare Beneficiary status.
good_looks_like: For each date of service the practice knows whether a nursing facility patient was in a Part A skilled stay, the stay Medicare pays the facility for.
Hospice election dates and the hospice's name are recorded the day they are learned.
Medicare Advantage enrollment and plan changes are caught by the monthly check.
Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries, low-income patients whose Medicare deductibles and coinsurance may not be billed to them, are flagged.
failure_modes: Every nursing facility visit gets one place-of-service code because nobody tracks Part A stays. Coding a Part A patient as a long-stay resident can create an overpayment that Medicare recovers.
A Medicare Advantage member elects hospice and claims keep going to the plan, which denies them.
A claim goes to Medicare when a workers' compensation or employer plan was primary.
Statements are sent to patients the practice is forbidden to bill.
In a Part A stay the practice bills Medicare for a test's technical part. With few exceptions, only professional services are separately payable. The facility pays for the rest.
key_questions: Do we know, for each nursing facility visit, whether the patient was in a Part A stay that day?
How do we learn that a patient has elected hospice, and how fast?
How many denials last quarter were for the wrong payer or for hospice?
Are Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries flagged in our system?

actions.action: Get skilled-stay status from each facility
actions.detail: A weekly census from the business office showing which residents are in a Part A stay, with start and end dates.

actions.action: Record hospice elections immediately
actions.detail: Election date, hospice name and whether the practice's clinician is the designated attending. Bill Original Medicare with modifier GV (attending, related care) or GW (unrelated care), even for Medicare Advantage members.

actions.action: Set place of service from status
actions.detail: Skilled nursing facility code (31) during a Part A stay, nursing facility code (32) otherwise, for each date of service. For 2026 visits the two codes pay differently. From 2027 visit codes pay the same.

actions.action: Flag patients who may not be billed
actions.detail: Mark Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries, suppress statements for Medicare cost sharing and refund anything already collected.

actions.action: Ask about coverage that pays before Medicare
actions.detail: At intake and each visit, ask the patient or representative about a current employer's plan, workers' compensation, and auto or liability insurance. Bill that payer first.

categories.applies_when: Essential for practices that see nursing facility or hospice patients, or patients with both Medicare and Medicaid. Office and hospital-based practices meet the same issues less often, mainly with Medicare Advantage switches and other primary payers such as workers' compensation or auto insurance.

vendor_refs.note: Requires a completed Medicare Secondary Payer questionnaire, a duty Medicare states for hospitals. Practices must ask about other coverage. Silent on hospice, Part A stays and protected beneficiaries.
Treats each Medicare Advantage plan as a separate payer with its own rules, which is right. It never mentions that Original Medicare pays once a plan member elects hospice.

categories.evidence_note: Medicare rules: place of service by Part A status (Claims Processing Manual chapter 12, section 30.6.13), hospice modifiers (chapter 11) and no billing of Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries. Federal auditors found $22.5 million overpaid in 2019 and 2020 on services coded 32 during Part A stays.

metrics.name: Denials for wrong payer or changed coverage status
metrics.definition: Share of claims denied because another payer was responsible, the patient was in a Medicare Advantage plan or hospice, or two payers had to settle which pays first.
metrics.formula: Claims denied for other-payer, managed-care, hospice or payer-order reasons / claims processed by payers
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. Track hospice and plan-switch denials as their own lines, since each has a specific upstream fix.
metrics.data_hint: Denial reason codes on the payment report: 22 (another payer may cover), 24 (covered by a managed care plan), 109 (send to the correct payer) and B9 (patient in hospice).

categories.name: Prior authorization and referrals
categories.summary: Knowing which services each payer will not pay for without advance approval or a referral, getting it, and recording the number on the claim. Mostly a Medicare Advantage, Medicaid plan and commercial issue. Original Medicare requires it for few services.
good_looks_like: A list by payer shows which of the practice's services need authorization or a referral.
Authorization is requested before the service, and the number, dates and units are stored with the encounter.
Expiring authorizations are flagged before they lapse.
Denials of authorization are appealed when the criteria were met.
failure_modes: A service is done on the assumption that the plan follows Medicare, and the claim is denied for no authorization.
An authorization was obtained but the number never reached the claim.
Visits continue after the approved dates or units ran out.
Denied requests are accepted without appeal. In Medicare Advantage in 2024, only 11.5% of denials were appealed, and 80.7% of appeals were overturned.
Staff assume Original Medicare never needs authorization. It does for some hospital outpatient procedures, equipment and ambulance trips, and since 2026 for selected services in a six-state pilot.
key_questions: Which of our services need authorization or a referral, for which plans?
How many claims were denied last quarter for missing authorization or referral?
Where is the authorization number stored, and does it reach the claim automatically?
Do we appeal authorization denials?

actions.action: List which services need approval, by payer
actions.detail: Start from last year's authorization and referral denials and each plan's published list. Note the source and the date last checked.

actions.action: Request before the service and record the number
actions.detail: Store approval number, dates and units where the claim can pick them up.

actions.action: Track expirations
actions.detail: A weekly list of authorizations ending in the next two weeks.

actions.action: Appeal denials that meet criteria
actions.detail: Send the clinical record that answers the plan's stated criteria point by point. Medicare Advantage plans must follow Medicare coverage rules and must give a specific reason for a denial.

actions.action: Cite the approval when a plan takes money back
actions.detail: A Medicare Advantage plan may not later deny a service it approved in advance for lack of medical necessity, except for good cause or fraud (42 CFR 422.138).

categories.applies_when: Practices with Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care, commercial or Veterans Affairs community care patients. Veterans Affairs must approve care in advance unless it is urgent or an emergency. Visits in hospitals and nursing facilities usually need no authorization of their own, though plans differ, and HMO (health maintenance organization) plans may require a referral from the assigned primary care physician.

vendor_refs.note: Sound register design: one record per request with owner, expiry date and outcome. Its 14-day turnaround assumptions predate the 2026 seven-day federal deadline. Its targets are unsourced.
Tracks approval number, approved code, dates and a match check, with no field for approved units. Its risk flag keeps finished cases flagged. The expiration list is filled by hand.
Warns that a plan may take money back for medical necessity after approving a service. Federal rule bars that except for good cause or fraud (42 CFR 422.138).
Its authorization list covers the top ten payers and twenty codes. Its claim that 50% to 65% of authorization denials are administrative has no source.

categories.evidence_note: Medicare Advantage denial and appeal rates are measured from 2024 plan reports. From 2026, Medicare Advantage and Medicaid plans must decide standard requests in seven calendar days and urgent ones in 72 hours (CMS-0057-F, 42 CFR 422.568, 422.572). Drugs, marketplace and employer plans are excluded.

metrics.name: Services requiring authorization that had one
metrics.definition: Share of encounters needing prior authorization or a referral for which approval was on file before the service.
metrics.formula: Encounters with authorization on file / encounters that required it
metrics.benchmark_note: The Healthcare Financial Management Association (HFMA) defines a similar measure with no target. HFMA also counts approvals obtained after the service but before the claim is sent. From first principles, aim for every such service.
metrics.data_hint: Authorization log matched to encounters. If the full list is unknown, count authorized encounters plus those denied for lack of authorization, as HFMA does.
metrics.vendor_claim: A staffing playbook in the purchased library sets a target of 98% or more for identifying required authorizations.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Unverifiable. No source is given, and HFMA publishes no target.

metrics.name: Denials for missing authorization or referral
metrics.definition: Share of claims denied because prior authorization or a required referral was absent or invalid.
metrics.formula: Claims denied for authorization or referral reasons / claims processed by payers
metrics.benchmark_note: No practice-level benchmark was found. For context, Medicare Advantage plans denied 7.7% of authorization requests in 2024. Only 11.5% of denials were appealed, and 80.7% of appeals succeeded (KFF, a health policy research group, from plan reports).
metrics.data_hint: Denial reason codes on the payment report: 197 (authorization absent), 198 (authorization exceeded), 284 and 296 (authorization does not match service or provider) and 288 (referral absent).
metrics.vendor_claim: The purchased front-end playbook sets authorization denials under 3% of all claims and flags over 5%. The Medicare Advantage playbook says under 5%.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Unverifiable. No source, and a share of all claims is not comparable between practices that need few authorizations and those that need many.

categories.name: Financial clearance, estimates and required notices
categories.summary: Telling patients the likely cost before a service, and delivering the notices the law requires: a good-faith estimate for uninsured and self-pay patients, and an Advance Beneficiary Notice when Original Medicare is expected to deny a service as not medically necessary.
good_looks_like: Self-pay and uninsured patients receive a written good-faith estimate within one business day of scheduling a service three or more business days ahead, or within three business days of asking.
Staff know which services need an Advance Beneficiary Notice and use the current form.
A written financial policy covers payment plans and hardship.
Hardship decisions are made case by case and documented.
A notice that self-pay patients can get an estimate is posted in the office and on the website.
failure_modes: A Medicare claim is denied as not medically necessary and, with no notice signed in advance, the patient cannot be billed.
The Medicare notice is used for Medicare Advantage patients, where it has no effect.
Medicare deductibles and coinsurance are waived routinely, which federal guidance treats as unlawful.
A self-pay patient is billed $400 or more above the estimate, which gives the patient a federal right to dispute the bill.
The Medicare notice is handed to every patient as routine. Medicare treats routine notices as ineffective.
key_questions: Which of our services are sometimes denied by Medicare as not medically necessary?
Do self-pay patients get a written estimate before scheduled services?
Is our financial hardship policy written, and are decisions documented?
Do we ever waive copayments or deductibles as a routine?
If our clinicians are out of network at a hospital where they work, do we ever bill insured patients more than their in-network share?

actions.action: List services that need a Medicare notice
actions.detail: Build it from the practice's own medical-necessity and frequency denials. Give the notice only when a denial is expected, to the patient or the legal representative, before the service.

actions.action: Give good-faith estimates to self-pay patients
actions.detail: Use the federal template. Send it within one business day of scheduling, or three business days of a request. Keep it with the medical record.

actions.action: Write a financial policy
actions.detail: Payment plans, hardship criteria and who may approve an exception.

actions.action: Never waive cost sharing routinely
actions.detail: Waive a patient's deductible, coinsurance or copayment only for documented individual hardship, after a good-faith effort to collect, or where the law forbids billing.

actions.action: Post the right-to-an-estimate notice
actions.detail: Display the federal model notice in the office, on the website and where scheduling happens, and tell self-pay patients when they book.

categories.applies_when: Mostly office and procedural practices with scheduled services and patient balances. The estimate rule does not cover Medicare or Medicaid patients, so practices doing hospital and facility visits for them rarely need it. A Medicare notice for a patient who cannot decide goes to the legal representative.

vendor_refs.note: Good idea: build the notice list from the practice's own denials. It wrongly puts the Medicare number on the form and says never-covered services need a notice to be billed.

States the estimate deadlines and the $400 dispute threshold correctly. Its penalty worksheet multiplies every missed estimate by the maximum fine, a worst case it presents as the practice's exposure.
Has usable scripts for stating the amount due. It never states the federal estimate duty or its deadlines, and never mentions Medicare or Medicaid.

categories.evidence_note: Federal requirements: good-faith estimates (45 CFR 149.610), the Medicare notice for Original Medicare only (Claims Processing Manual, chapter 30, section 50), and limits on out-of-network billing at in-network facilities (45 CFR 149.420). The routine-waiver warning is Inspector General guidance from 1994.

metrics.name: Self-pay services given a written estimate on time
metrics.definition: Share of services for uninsured or self-pay patients, scheduled at least 3 business days ahead or with an estimate requested, for which a written good-faith estimate was given on time.
metrics.formula: Qualifying self-pay services with an on-time estimate on file / qualifying self-pay services
metrics.benchmark_best: 100% of qualifying services, a legal requirement
metrics.benchmark_note: No survey benchmark was found. The target is the federal rule itself (45 CFR 149.610, text in effect November 2026): every self-pay service scheduled at least three business days ahead, and every request. Medicare and Medicaid patients are not counted.
metrics.data_hint: A copy of each estimate filed with the encounter.

categories.name: Time-of-service collections
categories.summary: Collecting copayments, deductibles and prior balances when the patient is present. What is not collected at the visit moves to statements and calls, which cost more and bring in less.
good_looks_like: Staff know what each patient owes before the visit, from the eligibility answer.
Copayments are requested at check-in as routine.
Several ways to pay exist, including a card on file with consent.
Collections are counted daily and compared with what was due.
failure_modes: Staff are uncomfortable asking, so copayments are billed later by statement, at extra cost and with less chance of payment.
The amount due is unknown at check-in because eligibility was not checked.
Cash and card receipts are not reconciled at day end.
Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries, who may not be charged Medicare deductibles or coinsurance, are asked to pay at the desk.
Estimated amounts are collected before the insurer has processed the claim, and the overpayments that result are not refunded.
key_questions: What share of copayments due do we collect at the visit?
Do staff know the amount due before the patient arrives?
Is the day's cash and card total reconciled every day?
If we have no front desk, what replaces this step?

actions.action: Show the amount due at check-in
actions.detail: Pull copayment and deductible from the eligibility answer onto the schedule.

actions.action: Train and script the request
actions.detail: A simple, consistent sentence, and a clear policy for patients who cannot pay that day.

actions.action: Offer card on file
actions.detail: With written consent and a stated maximum.

actions.action: Reconcile receipts daily
actions.detail: Cash, checks and card totals against the day's posting.

categories.applies_when: Office practices with a front desk. It does not apply to hospital and facility rounding, where no payment is collected at the visit. For nursing facility residents much of the patient's share is covered by a secondary payer or may not be billed. Those practices should measure what share of billable patient balances their statements collect.

vendor_refs.note: Good routine: show the amount, ask, coach each staff member. Its 90% target has no source, it calls copayments an absolute right, and never mentions Medicare or protected patients.
Scripts for quoting the amount at booking and check-in. It takes the copayment before rooming with no exceptions, which is wrong for patients who may not be charged.
Says visit-time collection costs nothing and later billing costs $8 to $14 a statement, with no source. Its 65% to 75% target conflicts with the library's other documents.

categories.evidence_note: The Medical Group Management Association (MGMA) measured the share of copayments and other balances collected at the visit (2024). The Healthcare Financial Management Association (HFMA) defines a different ratio, visit-time cash over all patient cash, with no target.

metrics.name: Point-of-service collection rate
metrics.definition: Share of patient amounts due at the time of the visit, such as copayments, that were collected at the visit.
metrics.formula: Patient payments collected at the visit / patient amounts due at the visit
metrics.benchmark_typical: 72% of copayments, 27% of other balances due
metrics.benchmark_note: MGMA, 2024 data, quoted in a July 2026 article without method detail: practices collected 72% of copayments and about 27% of other balances at the time of service. HFMA defines a different ratio, against all self-pay cash, with no target.
metrics.data_hint: Daily collection log compared with copayments due on the schedule.
metrics.vendor_claim: The purchased library gives three different targets: over 90% of known patient amounts in its measure guides, 65% to 75% in its front-end playbook, and 95% or more of copayments.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Unverifiable. No source is cited and the targets disagree. Measured reality is far lower: 72% of copayments in 2024 (MGMA).
